demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about why the event has happened to me
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

issues.item: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy items imply an ongoing external danger/escape-monitoring profile more typical of fear-based threat from assault, accident re-exposure, or unsafe environments. That does not fit well with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another,' where the central disturbance is more plausibly guilt, responsibility, and intrusive memory rather than escape positioning.

Mirror checking is not clinically coherent with the rest of this profile. For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another, the other selected items center on dissociative/fragmented memory and guilt-focused rumination/meaning seeking. Mirror checking instead suggests appearance/body/reality checking behavior that is not supported by the memory items, not linked by the formulation's active edges, and is hard to explain as part of the same PTSD presentation here.

vignette: Jane, a 61-year-old single woman of Oceania descent, has worked as a security guard for over two decades. Her life took an unexpected and harrowing turn when she accidentally caused a serious injury to another person at work. The incident occurred during her night shift, where she was assigned to patrol the parking lot of a large office complex. One evening, while checking for unauthorized vehicles, Jane noticed a car parked in a restricted area. As she approached the vehicle to place a warning notice, she heard a sudden noise behind her-a fellow security guard attempting to walk through the same gate without his flashlight on. In an attempt to alert him and prevent him from tripping over some loose wires, Jane yelled out a warning, but her movement caused the car alarm to go off loudly. The loud sound startled both of them, and in the confusion, the other guard stumbled and fell into an open manhole that had been left unsecured due to ongoing maintenance. The immediate aftermath was chaotic as Jane tried to help the injured guard while simultaneously calling for emergency services. Despite her efforts, she could not prevent him from sustaining severe injuries. Since then, Jane has become consumed by self-blame and a relentless quest for meaning in what happened that night. Jane often thinks about why this event had to happen to her and how it might have been prevented. She dwells on the moments leading up to the accident, repeatedly analyzing each detail with an obsessive intensity. The question of whether she could have done something differently haunts her daily life. Her mind replays the sequence of events over and over again, but no matter how many times she goes through it, she cannot escape the feeling that she bears some responsibility. The memory itself is fragmented; there are significant gaps in what she can recall about the night of the incident. When she does remember parts of it, they feel disconnected from her own experience, as if someone else had lived them. She has trouble attaching any emotional weight to these recollections, and sometimes feels completely numb when recounting the event, as though she is a bystander observing something that happened to another person. These fragmented memories and her emotional detachment have led Jane into a pattern of avoidance. She avoids going back to the parking lot where the incident occurred and tries not to be alone at night shifts. This behavior has started to impact her work; her supervisors have noticed a decline in her performance as she often appears distracted or absent-minded during patrols. Jane's personal life has also been affected. Her single status means that she spends much of her time alone, which exacerbates her tendency to ruminate on the incident. She finds it difficult to connect with others and share what happened because even recounting the event feels unreal and painful. The culmination of these experiences finally prompted Jane to seek help. She realized that her mental state was deteriorating, affecting both her job performance and her overall well-being. What frightens her most is the fear of being defined by this single incident for the rest of her life. At the same time, she hopes for a way to understand what happened without feeling like it overshadows everything else in her existence. In therapy sessions, Jane has expressed that she is searching for some form of closure or understanding-something that can help her reconcile the event with her sense of self and move forward. Her journey towards healing involves finding meaning in this tragic turn of events while also addressing the intense feelings of guilt and self-blame that have taken root within her.
